name: PERCENTILE.EXC
description: PERCENTILE.EXC returns the k-th percentile using the exclusive method, where k must be strictly between 0 and 1, so the result never equals the minimum or maximum.
tldr: Returns the value at percentile k (0 < k < 1) using the exclusive method.

parameters.name: array
parameters.description: The range or array of numeric values.

parameters.name: k
parameters.description: The percentile, a number strictly between 0 and 1 (e.g. 0.25, 0.75).

basicExample.explanation: Rank = 0.25*(6+1) = 1.75; interpolate 75% from the 1st to the 2nd value: 1 + 0.75*(2-1) = 1.75.

advancedExamples.title: 75th percentile of six values
advancedExamples.description: The exclusive rank places the percentile inside the data range.
advancedExamples.explanation: Rank = 0.75*(6+1) = 5.25; interpolate 25% from the 5th to the 6th value: 5 + 0.25*(6-5) = 5.25.

advancedExamples.title: k at the edge is rejected
advancedExamples.description: The exclusive method requires k strictly between 0 and 1, so the extremes are invalid.
advancedExamples.explanation: k = 0 is not allowed; the exclusive method cannot return the minimum.

howItWorks: PERCENTILE.EXC uses the exclusive (EXC) method. It computes a rank as k*(n+1), where n is the count of values, then linearly interpolates between the surrounding sorted values. Because k is strictly between 0 and 1, the result always lies strictly between the minimum and maximum. k must fall in the open interval (1/(n+1), n/(n+1)); values outside this range return #NUM!. Text and logical values are ignored.

howToSteps.name: Select the result cell
howToSteps.text: Click where you want the percentile.

howToSteps.name: Enter the formula
howToSteps.text: Type =PERCENTILE.EXC(range, k) with k strictly between 0 and 1.

howToSteps.name: Press Enter
howToSteps.text: The interpolated percentile value is returned.

limitations: k must be strictly between 0 and 1; k = 0 or k = 1 cause #NUM!.
Only certain k values are valid; k must be in (1/(n+1), n/(n+1)) or #NUM! occurs.
Interpolates, so the result is generally not an actual data value.

commonErrors.cause: k is 0 or 1, or k is outside the valid range (1/(n+1), n/(n+1)).
commonErrors.fix: Use a k strictly between 0 and 1, or switch to PERCENTILE.INC if you need the minimum or maximum.

commonErrors.cause: The two functions use different interpolation formulas.
commonErrors.fix: Choose .INC when you need inclusive 0..1 bounds; .EXC otherwise.

googleSheetsEquivalent.description: Google Sheets supports PERCENTILE.EXC with the same exclusive behavior as Excel 2010+.

faq.question: What is the difference between .INC and .EXC?
faq.answer: .INC allows k from 0 to 1 and uses rank 1 + k*(n-1), potentially returning the min or max. .EXC requires k strictly between 0 and 1 and uses rank k*(n+1), so it never returns the min or max.

faq.question: Why do I get #NUM! with k = 0.1 on a small list?
faq.answer: On a small dataset the valid range (1/(n+1), n/(n+1)) may exclude small k; for n=6, k must be above 1/7 (~0.143).

faq.question: When should I use PERCENTILE.EXC?
faq.answer: Use it when your statistical definition requires excluding the endpoints, such as certain textbook percentile formulas.
